newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Afghan Taleban refuse peace talks offer.
newsitem.headline: Afghan Taleban refuse peace talks offer.

text.p: Afghanistan's fundamentalist Islamic Taleban rejected on Monday an offer of peace talks from the Uzbek militia leader Abdul Rashid Dostum, saying the invitation was an insult.
"When the enemy was defeated, they launched this offer to waste time and keep the opposition busy." Acting Information Minister Amir Khan Mutaqi told a news conference.

"We do not want to take part in negotiations which we believe will have no result." Mutaqi said. Dostum heads an anti-Taleban alliance, which also includes forces led by Ahmad Shah Masood, the military chief of the ousted President Burhanuddin Rabbani.

Dostum had invited all religious and political parties to his stronghold of Mazar-e-Sharif in northern Afghanistan to discuss the future of the country. The offer was reported by the British Broadcasting Corporation on Sunday.
Mutaqi said the fact that the meetings would be chaired by Dostum, who once served the communist regime in Afghanistan, was an insult.

"Dostum has a bad record. We who call ourselves mujahideen (holy warriors) and Taleban consider our participation in any sort of meeting which is supposed to be headed by Dostum as an insult to Islam and to ourselves." said Mutaqi.
He also called on all other parties who fought a Moscow-backed communist regime in the 1980s to boycott the meeting.
Mutaqi did leave the door open for talks, but indicated there would be no compromise on the Taleban aim of spreading Islam's stern Sharia law to the entire country.

"We are ready to talk to them providing they agree on the conditions of a ceasefire and an exchange of prisoners of war. It also should be clear that the meetings should have some sort of result." he said.
"We are ready to negotiate with anybody who accepts our principles," he added.

The United Nations, the Organisation of the Islamic Conference and surrounding nations have been trying to bring the warring factions together for negotiations since the fall of the communist government in 1992, so far with little success.
Mutaqi also used the news conference to accuse Iran, India and Russia of helping the alliance formed by Dostum and Masood.
"When (the ex-government) held Kabul, they were given arms by Iran and India, and also Indian technicians were helping them. The Russians were giving them ammunition," he said.
"Some attacks have been launched from across the Iranian border, and a limited number of men have been trained in Iran."
Accusations of foreign support are frequently traded by the opposing factions. No side in the war has admitted to receiving military help from foreign countries.
Dostum's offer of peace talks came as the two sides were deadlocked in fighting over hills 25 to 30 km (15 to 19 miles) north of Kabul.
There is also fighting in the remote northwestern province of Badghis. Both sides claim control of the region, which is the gateway to the western city of Herat near the Iranian border.
At least two bombs were dropped on the airport in Herat on Monday morning, reliable sources said. There were no reports of damage.

Mutaqi accused Dostum of launching the attacks, similar to a series of bombing raids on the airport on the northeastern edge of Kabul, which, like Herat, is used for military as well as civilian traffic.
None of the bombs damaged Kabul airport, although two apparently aimed at a military base in a northwestern suburb destroyed two houses, killed three children and wounded seven people.
